```{python}
#| label: setup

import matplotlib.ticker as mticker
import seaborn as sns

from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller
from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf, plot_pacf
from statsmodels.stats.diagnostic import acorr_ljungbox, het_arch
from statsmodels.graphics.gofplots import qqplot
import mplfinance as mpf
import joypy

TICKERS = ["SPY", "AAPL", "MSFT", "JPM", "XOM", "JNJ", "KO", "TSLA"]

TICKER_COLORS = {
    "SPY": "#2a78d6",
    "AAPL": "#eb6834",
    "MSFT": "#1baf7a",
    "JPM": "#eda100",
    "XOM": "#e87ba4",
    "JNJ": "#008300",

}

SEQUENTIAL_RAMP = ["#cde2fb", "#86b6ef", "#3987e5", "#2a78d6", "#1c5cab", "#0d366b"]
DIVERGING_BLUE_RED = ["#0d366b", "#2a78d6", "#f0efec", "#e34948", "#8a1f1f"]

COLOR_GRID = "#e1e0d9"
COLOR_MUTED = "#898781"
COLOR_SECONDARY_INK = "#52514e"
COLOR_PRIMARY_INK = "#0b0b0b"
COLOR_SURFACE = "#fcfcfb"


def set_financial_theme():
    sns.set_theme(style="white")
    plt.rcParams.update({
        "figure.facecolor": COLOR_SURFACE,
        "axes.facecolor": COLOR_SURFACE,
        "savefig.facecolor": COLOR_SURFACE,
        "axes.edgecolor": COLOR_GRID,
        "axes.grid": True,
        "grid.color": COLOR_GRID,
        "grid.linewidth": 0.6,
        "axes.spines.top": False,
        "axes.spines.right": False,
        "axes.spines.left": False,
        "axes.spines.bottom": False,
        "xtick.color": COLOR_MUTED,
        "ytick.color": COLOR_MUTED,
        "text.color": COLOR_SECONDARY_INK,
        "axes.labelcolor": COLOR_SECONDARY_INK,
        "axes.titlecolor": COLOR_PRIMARY_INK,
        "axes.titleweight": "bold",
        "axes.titlesize": 14,
        "font.size": 11,
        "legend.frameon": False,
        "legend.labelcolor": COLOR_SECONDARY_INK,
    })


set_financial_theme()


def style_table(df, formats=None):
    styler = df.style.hide(axis="index")
    if formats:
        styler = styler.format(formats)
    styler = styler.set_table_styles([
        {"selector": "th", "props": [
            ("background-color", COLOR_SURFACE), ("color", COLOR_SECONDARY_INK),
            ("border-bottom", f"1px solid {COLOR_GRID}"), ("text-align", "right"),
            ("padding", "6px 10px"),
        ]},
        {"selector": "td", "props": [
            ("border-bottom", f"1px solid {COLOR_GRID}"), ("padding", "6px 10px"),
            ("color", COLOR_PRIMARY_INK),
        ]},
    ]).set_properties(**{"text-align": "right"})
    return styler


def add_title(ax, title, subtitle=None):
    ax.set_title(title, loc="left", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=COLOR_PRIMARY_INK, pad=26 if subtitle else 10)
    if subtitle:
        ax.text(0.0, 1.02, subtitle, transform=ax.transAxes, fontsize=10.5, color=COLOR_SECONDARY_INK, va="bottom")


prices = pd.read_csv("data/prices.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).sort_values(["ticker", "date"])
spy_ohlcv = pd.read_csv("data/spy_ohlcv.csv", parse_dates=["date"]).sort_values("date")

prices["log_return"] = prices.groupby("ticker")["adj_close"].transform(lambda x: np.log(x / x.shift(1)))
returns = prices.dropna(subset=["log_return"]).reset_index(drop=True)
```

## Executive Summary {.unnumbered}

Daily returns for SPY and seven sector-diverse stocks are not normally distributed,
and the gap has real consequences, not just a technical footnote. Every ticker
shows significant excess kurtosis (SPY highest at 13.2, TSLA lowest at 4.7), and
three independent normality tests reject the normal distribution for all 8 tickers
by many orders of magnitude, easily surviving a Bonferroni correction; a
4-standard-deviation SPY day happens roughly 120 times more often than a normal
distribution predicts. Volatility is not constant either: SPY's annualized
volatility spiked as high as 94% during the 2020 COVID crash, 7.6 times its 12.3%
typical level, and a GARCH(1,1) model using only one day of memory (96%
persistence) tracks that swing closely, something an iid-normal assumption rules
out entirely. The consequence shows up directly in Value-at-Risk: a
normal-distribution VaR model breaches its own 99% confidence threshold 1.8 to 2.6
times more often than it should, on every one of the 8 tickers, and for SPY
specifically understates the 1-in-100-day loss on a $1M position by roughly 25%, or
$5,752. An empirical (historical) VaR model does meaningfully better but is not
perfect either, and Christoffersen's test shows breaches cluster in time under both
methods rather than landing independently, the same volatility-clustering signature
from Sections 5 and 6 showing up again inside a risk model's own failures.

```{python}
#| label: fig-executive-summary
#| fig-cap: "99% VaR breach rate as a multiple of the 1% nominal rate, all 8 tickers"
#| echo: false

summary_var_results = []
for ticker in TICKERS:
    series = returns.loc[returns["ticker"] == ticker].sort_values("date").set_index("date")["log_return"]
    mu = series.rolling(252).mean().shift(1)
    sigma = series.rolling(252).std().shift(1)
    normal_threshold = mu + stats.norm.ppf(0.01) * sigma
    historical_threshold = series.rolling(252).quantile(0.01).shift(1)
    valid = normal_threshold.notna()
    actual, normal_threshold, historical_threshold = series[valid], normal_threshold[valid], historical_threshold[valid]
    summary_var_results.append({
        "ticker": ticker,
        "normal_ratio": (actual < normal_threshold).mean() / 0.01,
        "historical_ratio": (actual < historical_threshold).mean() / 0.01,
    })
summary_var_results = pd.DataFrame(summary_var_results)

x_pos = np.arange(len(TICKERS))
width = 0.38

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(x_pos - width / 2, summary_var_results["normal_ratio"], width, color=COLOR_MUTED, label="Normal VaR")
ax.bar(x_pos + width / 2, summary_var_results["historical_ratio"], width, color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], label="Historical VaR")
ax.axhline(1.0, color=COLOR_PRIMARY_INK, linewidth=1, linestyle=":", label="Perfectly calibrated")
ax.set_xticks(x_pos)
ax.set_xticklabels(TICKERS)
ax.set_ylabel("Actual breach rate / 1% nominal rate")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
add_title(ax, "A Normal-Distribution Risk Model Fails on Every Single Ticker", "99% VaR breach rate as a multiple of the nominal rate, all 8 tickers")
fig.tight_layout()
```

## Introduction

This report asks a simple question: do daily returns for a major stock market index
and a sector-diverse set of individual stocks look normally distributed, and what
happens to models that assume they do. The data covers SPY, the S&P 500 index fund,
alongside seven individual stocks chosen for sector spread rather than similarity:
AAPL and MSFT (technology), JPM (financials), XOM (energy), JNJ (healthcare), KO
(consumer staples), and TSLA (high-volatility growth). Daily prices run from
January 2011 through the most recent trading day, roughly fifteen years, covering
both calm periods and two sharp volatility episodes, the 2020 COVID crash and the
2022 rate-hiking cycle.

The analysis proceeds in stages. First, a visual pass at whether the return
distributions look normal at a glance. Second, formal statistical tests of that
question. Third, whether volatility is constant over time or clusters into calm and
turbulent periods. Fourth, whether daily returns are independent of each other or
carry statistical memory. Each of these has a direct consequence for risk models,
and the final section quantifies that consequence for Value-at-Risk, a widely used
measure of how much a position could lose in a single day.

## Data

Prices come from Yahoo Finance via the `yfinance` package [@yfinance], adjusted for
splits and dividends. All 8 tickers have identical coverage: 3,952 trading days from 2011-01-03
to the most recent close, with no missing values in any series. Log returns are
computed as the day-over-day change in log price, which leaves 3,951 return
observations per ticker (the first day of the window has no prior price to compare
against). The table below summarizes the daily log return distribution for each
ticker before any shape or normality question is asked of it.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-summary-stats
#| tbl-cap: "Daily log return summary statistics by ticker"

summary_stats = (
    returns.groupby("ticker")["log_return"]
    .agg(n="count", mean="mean", std="std", min="min", max="max")
    .reindex(TICKERS)
    .reset_index()
)

style_table(summary_stats, formats={
    "n": "{:,.0f}",
    "mean": "{:.4%}",
    "std": "{:.4%}",
    "min": "{:.2%}",
    "max": "{:.2%}",
})
```

Before any autocorrelation or volatility analysis can be trusted, the return series
themselves need to be stationary, meaning their statistical properties do not drift
systematically over time. This is standard practice to check rather than assume. The
Augmented Dickey-Fuller test [@dickey1979] does this by testing whether a series has
a unit root (a tendency to wander rather than revert); rejecting that null hypothesis
is evidence of stationarity.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What is the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test?"}
A stationary series is one whose statistical properties, like its mean and variance,
do not drift systematically over time. A series with a unit root instead tends to
wander: today's level depends heavily on yesterday's level plus a shock that never
fully fades, so shocks accumulate rather than dissipate. The test fits

$$
\Delta y_t = \alpha + \beta y_{t-1} + \sum_{i=1}^{p} \phi_i \Delta y_{t-i} + \varepsilon_t
$$

where $\Delta y_t = y_t - y_{t-1}$, and checks whether $\beta$ is significantly less
than zero: the lagged-difference terms soak up any short-term autocorrelation so the
test on $\beta$ isolates the unit-root question. A large negative test statistic and
a small p-value reject the null of $\beta = 0$ (a unit root) and support
stationarity.
:::

```{python}
#| label: tbl-adf
#| tbl-cap: "Augmented Dickey-Fuller stationarity test on daily log returns"

adf_results = []
for ticker in TICKERS:
    series = returns.loc[returns["ticker"] == ticker, "log_return"]
    stat, pvalue, *_ = adfuller(series, autolag="AIC")
    adf_results.append({"ticker": ticker, "adf_statistic": stat, "p_value": pvalue})

adf_table = pd.DataFrame(adf_results)

style_table(adf_table, formats={"adf_statistic": "{:.2f}", "p_value": "{:.4f}"})
```

Every ticker rejects the unit-root null at any conventional threshold: even judged
against a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.05 divided by 8 (0.00625), to account
for running the same test 8 times, every p-value clears it by many orders of
magnitude. All 8 log return series are treated as stationary for the rest of this
report.

Finally, the sector spread behind these 8 tickers was chosen deliberately, not
arbitrarily, so it is worth checking directly: are these return series actually
distinct from each other, or do they move together closely enough that "8 tickers"
is really just one story repeated 8 times. The heatmap below shows the pairwise
correlation of daily log returns.

```{python}
#| label: fig-correlation-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise correlation of daily log returns across all 8 tickers"

from matplotlib.colors import LinearSegmentedColormap

diverging_cmap = LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("diverging_blue_red", DIVERGING_BLUE_RED)

corr_matrix = wide_prices.pct_change().apply(lambda x: np.log1p(x)).corr().reindex(index=TICKERS, columns=TICKERS)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 7))
sns.heatmap(
    corr_matrix, annot=True, fmt=".2f", cmap=diverging_cmap, vmin=-1, vmax=1,
    center=0, square=True, linewidths=1, linecolor=COLOR_SURFACE,
    cbar_kws={"label": "Correlation"}, ax=ax,
)
ax.set_xlabel(None)
ax.set_ylabel(None)
add_title(ax, "SPY Correlates Most With Its Largest Holdings", "Pairwise correlation of daily log returns, 2011 to present")
fig.tight_layout()
```

SPY's three strongest correlations are with MSFT (0.73), JPM (0.73), and AAPL (0.68),
consistent with SPY being a market-cap-weighted index that these large-cap names
have real weight in. The weakest pair in the entire matrix is JNJ and TSLA (0.10),
a healthcare staple and a high-volatility growth stock, about as different as two
equities get. Averaged across its correlation with the other 7 tickers, TSLA sits
lowest at 0.27, well below SPY's average of 0.59, so TSLA is the ticker that moves
most independently of the rest of the set. No pair is close to perfectly correlated,
confirming the sector spread is doing real work rather than sampling eight versions
of the same underlying signal.

## Distributional Shape at a Glance

Before running any formal test, it is worth asking what a return distribution looks
like next to a normal curve with the same center and spread. Two properties matter
most here: skewness, whether the distribution leans to one side, and kurtosis, how
much probability sits in the tails and the peak compared to a normal distribution.
D'Agostino's skewness test and kurtosis test [@dagostino1973] give an inferential
read on both, across all 8 tickers, before the fuller Jarque-Bera and Shapiro-Wilk
treatment in the next section.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What do skewness and kurtosis measure?"}
Skewness measures asymmetry: a symmetric distribution, like the normal, has zero
skewness, a positive value means a longer right tail, a negative value means a
longer left tail. Kurtosis measures how much probability sits in the tails and the
peak relative to a normal distribution; the normal distribution has a kurtosis of 3,
so this report reports "excess kurtosis" (kurtosis minus 3), where zero matches a
normal distribution and a positive value means fatter tails and a sharper peak than
normal. D'Agostino's skewness test and kurtosis test each check whether the sample's
value on that one property is far enough from what a normal distribution would
produce to rule out normality on that property alone.
:::

```{python}
#| label: tbl-skew-kurtosis
#| tbl-cap: "D'Agostino skewness and kurtosis tests on daily log returns"

shape_results = []
for ticker in TICKERS:
    series = returns.loc[returns["ticker"] == ticker, "log_return"]
    skew_stat, skew_p = stats.skewtest(series)
    kurt_stat, kurt_p = stats.kurtosistest(series)
    shape_results.append({
        "ticker": ticker,
        "excess_kurtosis": stats.kurtosis(series),
        "skewtest_p": skew_p,
        "kurtosistest_p": kurt_p,
    })

shape_table = pd.DataFrame(shape_results)

style_table(shape_table, formats={"excess_kurtosis": "{:.2f}", "skewtest_p": "{:.4f}", "kurtosistest_p": "{:.4f}"})
```

Every ticker's excess kurtosis is positive, and the kurtosis test rejects normal-level
kurtosis for all 8 at any conventional threshold, so the "fatter peak, fatter tails"
shape is universal in this data. This section runs 16 tests (8 tickers x 2
properties), so the relevant Bonferroni-adjusted threshold is 0.05 divided by 16, or
0.003125, not the uncorrected 0.05: every kurtosis p-value clears it trivially.
Skewness is a different story: only 6 of the 8 tickers (SPY, AAPL, JPM, XOM, JNJ,
KO) show statistically significant skew, and one of those six is a genuine
near-miss, JPM's skew p-value of 0.00307 survives the 0.003125 threshold by less
than 2%, closer to a coin flip than the other five tickers' skew results. MSFT
(p = 0.44) and TSLA (p = 0.61) do not reject the null of a symmetric distribution at
any threshold.
Kurtosis, not skewness, is the consistent shape violation here.

The chart below puts that kurtosis number in visual form for SPY specifically: its
daily log returns against a normal curve fit with the exact same mean and standard
deviation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-spy-histogram-normal
#| fig-cap: "SPY daily log returns vs. a normal curve with the same mean and standard deviation"

spy_returns = returns.loc[returns["ticker"] == "SPY", "log_return"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(spy_returns, bins=80, density=True, color=SEQUENTIAL_RAMP[3], edgecolor=COLOR_SURFACE, linewidth=0.3, label="Empirical")
x_grid = np.linspace(spy_returns.min(), spy_returns.max(), 300)
ax.plot(x_grid, stats.norm.pdf(x_grid, spy_returns.mean(), spy_returns.std()), color=COLOR_PRIMARY_INK, linewidth=1.8, label="Normal fit")
ax.set_xlabel("Daily log return")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
add_title(ax, "SPY's Returns Are Sharper-Peaked and Longer-Tailed Than Normal", "Excess kurtosis of 13.2 against a normal curve with the same mean and std")
fig.tight_layout()
```

The SPY-only chart above raises an obvious question: is this an SPY quirk, or does
it hold across every ticker in the set. The small-multiples grid below repeats the
same histogram-and-normal-curve treatment for all 8, each on its own independent
axis so its individual shape is visible regardless of how its volatility compares
to the others.

```{python}
#| label: fig-histogram-grid
#| fig-cap: "Daily log returns vs. fitted normal curve, all 8 tickers"

fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 4, figsize=(12, 6))
for ax, ticker in zip(axs.flat, TICKERS):
    series = returns.loc[returns["ticker"] == ticker, "log_return"]
    ax.hist(series, bins=50, density=True, color=TICKER_COLORS[ticker], edgecolor=COLOR_SURFACE, linewidth=0.2)
    x_grid = np.linspace(series.min(), series.max(), 200)
    ax.plot(x_grid, stats.norm.pdf(x_grid, series.mean(), series.std()), color=COLOR_PRIMARY_INK, linewidth=1.2)
    ax.set_title(ticker, loc="left", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=COLOR_SECONDARY_INK, pad=6)
    ax.set_yticklabels([])
    ax.set_ylabel(None)

fig.suptitle("Every Ticker Is More Fat-Tailed and Peaked Than a Normal Curve", x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=COLOR_PRIMARY_INK)
fig.text(0.01, 0.93, "Independent x and y axes per panel; shape, not scale, is what to compare", fontsize=10.5, color=COLOR_SECONDARY_INK)
fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.88])
```

A ridgeline plot makes the same comparison more compact, stacking all 8 distributions
on a shared, standardized x-axis (each ticker's returns converted to standard
deviations from its own mean) so shape, and only shape, is what differs between rows.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How to read a ridgeline plot"}
Each row is a separate density curve, a smoothed version of a histogram, for one
ticker's return distribution, stacked so all 8 can be compared without an
eight-color legend-heavy overlay. Taller and narrower means more of that ticker's
returns cluster tightly around its center; curves that stay visibly above zero
further out along the x-axis before flattening mean more extreme values occur, even
if rarely. Overlap between rows is intentional, it is what makes the stack compact,
not a sign anything is misaligned.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-ridgeline
#| fig-cap: "Standardized daily log returns for all 8 tickers"

returns_ridgeline = returns.copy()
returns_ridgeline["standardized_return"] = returns_ridgeline.groupby("ticker")["log_return"].transform(lambda x: (x - x.mean()) / x.std())
returns_ridgeline["ticker"] = pd.Categorical(returns_ridgeline["ticker"], categories=TICKERS, ordered=True)

fig, axes = joypy.joyplot(
    returns_ridgeline, by="ticker", column="standardized_return",
    color=[TICKER_COLORS[t] for t in TICKERS],
    figsize=(12, 8), overlap=0.7, x_range=[-6, 6], grid=False,
    linecolor=COLOR_SURFACE, linewidth=1,
)
add_title(axes[0], "Fat Tails Are the Rule Across All 8 Tickers, Not an SPY Exception", "Standardized daily log returns (standard deviations from each ticker's own mean)")
fig.subplots_adjust(top=0.88)
```

Both charts above show peakedness and tail weight, but neither one quantifies how
much more often an extreme move actually happens than a normal distribution would
predict. The chart below answers that directly for SPY: the probability of a daily
move exceeding a given number of standard deviations, empirical against
normal-implied, on a log scale so the gap at the extremes is visible instead of
compressed to zero.

```{python}
#| label: fig-fat-tails-log
#| fig-cap: "SPY: empirical vs. normal-implied probability of a daily move exceeding N standard deviations"

spy_z = (spy_returns - spy_returns.mean()) / spy_returns.std()
thresholds = np.arange(1, 8.01, 0.25)
empirical_p = [np.mean(spy_z.abs() > t) for t in thresholds]
normal_p = [2 * (1 - stats.norm.cdf(t)) for t in thresholds]

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(thresholds, empirical_p, color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], linewidth=2, label="Empirical (SPY)")
ax.plot(thresholds, normal_p, color=COLOR_MUTED, linewidth=2, linestyle="--", label="Normal-implied")
ax.set_yscale("log")
ax.set_xlabel("Move size (standard deviations)")
ax.set_ylabel("P(|daily return| > threshold), log scale")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
add_title(ax, "A 4-Sigma SPY Day Happens 120 Times More Often Than Normal Predicts", "Empirical vs. normal-implied tail probability, log scale")
fig.tight_layout()
```

At 2 standard deviations the empirical and normal-implied probabilities are close,
4.6% against 4.5%. The gap opens fast after that: at 4 standard deviations, SPY's
actual probability of a move that large is 120 times what a normal distribution
would predict, and at 5 standard deviations the ratio is roughly 4,900 times. The
single most extreme day in the entire 15-year window is 2020-03-16, a -11.6% day at
the height of the COVID crash, a -10.8 standard deviation move that a normal
distribution would predict roughly once every 10^26 trading days, which is to say,
never.

## Formal Normality Tests

Section 3 built a visual and light inferential case that these returns are not
normal. This section runs three formal, widely used normality tests on all 8
tickers: Jarque-Bera [@jarquebera1980], which tests skewness and kurtosis jointly;
Shapiro-Wilk [@shapirowilk1965], which tests the full shape of the distribution and
is generally considered one of the most powerful normality tests available; and
Anderson-Darling [@andersondarling1952], which weights deviations in the tails more
heavily than the center, making it especially sensitive to exactly
the kind of tail behavior Section 3 raised.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What do these three normality tests actually test?"}
All three test the same null hypothesis, that the data came from a normal
distribution, but check different things. Jarque-Bera combines a sample's skewness
$S$ and excess kurtosis $K$ into a single chi-square statistic:

$$
JB = \frac{n}{6}\left(S^2 + \frac{K^2}{4}\right)
$$

where $n$ is the sample size; large deviations in either skewness or kurtosis push
$JB$ up and the p-value down, and both are weighted so that kurtosis (squared and
divided by 4) has to deviate less than skewness to move the statistic by the same
amount, reflecting how much more informative excess kurtosis is for fat tails.
Shapiro-Wilk compares the correlation between the sample's sorted values and the
values a normal distribution would be expected to produce at those same ranks; a
perfectly normal sample would correlate at 1.0, and the test statistic $W$ falls as
the fit worsens. Anderson-Darling is built from the same family as the more familiar
Kolmogorov-Smirnov test but weights deviations in the tails more heavily than
deviations near the center, which is why it does not report a simple p-value here:
instead its statistic is compared against a critical value tabulated for a chosen
significance level (1% in this report), and exceeding that critical value rejects
normality at that level.
:::

```{python}
#| label: tbl-normality-tests
#| tbl-cap: "Jarque-Bera, Shapiro-Wilk, and Anderson-Darling normality tests on daily log returns"

normality_results = []
for ticker in TICKERS:
    series = returns.loc[returns["ticker"] == ticker, "log_return"]
    jb_stat, jb_p = stats.jarque_bera(series)
    sh_stat, sh_p = stats.shapiro(series)
    ad_result = stats.anderson(series, dist="norm")
    ad_critical_1pct = ad_result.critical_values[-1]
    normality_results.append({
        "ticker": ticker,
        "jarque_bera": jb_stat,
        "jb_p": jb_p,
        "shapiro_w": sh_stat,
        "shapiro_p": sh_p,
        "anderson_darling": ad_result.statistic,
        "ad_critical_1pct": ad_critical_1pct,
        "rejects_at_1pct": "Yes" if ad_result.statistic > ad_critical_1pct else "No",
    })

normality_table = pd.DataFrame(normality_results)

style_table(normality_table, formats={
    "jarque_bera": "{:,.0f}", "jb_p": "{:.4f}",
    "shapiro_w": "{:.4f}", "shapiro_p": "{:.4f}",
    "anderson_darling": "{:.2f}", "ad_critical_1pct": "{:.3f}",
})
```

Every ticker rejects normality on every one of the three tests. The Jarque-Bera and
Shapiro-Wilk p-values are effectively zero for all 8, not just below 0.05, and every
Anderson-Darling statistic is 35 to 65 times larger than its own 1% critical value of
1.091, nowhere close to a borderline call. This section runs 24 tests, not 8: three
test types across 8 tickers each. Judged per-ticker against a Bonferroni-adjusted
threshold of 0.05 divided by 8 (0.00625), or against the stricter full-family
threshold of 0.05 divided by 24 (0.00208), every p-value here clears either bar by
dozens of orders of magnitude, so the multiplicity correction changes nothing about
the conclusion under any reasonable framing: this is not a marginal,
multiplicity-driven result.

A single p-value cannot show where a distribution departs from normal, only that it
does. The QQ plot below shows SPY's actual return quantiles against the quantiles a
normal distribution would produce; departure from the diagonal reference line marks
exactly where the mismatch happens.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How to read a QQ plot"}
A QQ (quantile-quantile) plot sorts the actual data from smallest to largest and
plots each value against the value a normal distribution would be expected to
produce at that same percentile. If the data were exactly normal, every point would
fall on the diagonal reference line. Points curving away from the line at the low
end mean the data's smallest values are more extreme than normal predicts; points
curving away at the high end mean the same for the largest values. Both ends bowing
away, as they do here, is the QQ-plot signature of fat tails.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-qq-plot
#| fig-cap: "QQ plot of SPY daily log returns against a normal distribution"

(osm, osr), (slope, intercept, r) = stats.probplot(spy_returns, dist="norm")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter(osm, osr, s=12, color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], alpha=0.6, label="SPY quantiles")
ax.plot(osm, slope * osm + intercept, color=COLOR_PRIMARY_INK, linewidth=1.5, label="Normal reference line")
ax.set_xlabel("Theoretical quantiles (normal)")
ax.set_ylabel("Sample quantiles (SPY daily log return)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
add_title(ax, "SPY's Tails Bow Sharply Away From the Normal Reference Line", "QQ plot, both ends departing from the diagonal is the fat-tails signature")
fig.tight_layout()
```

Both tails curl away from the reference line rather than hugging it, the QQ-plot
signature of a fat-tailed distribution: the most extreme empirical quantiles are far
more extreme than a normal distribution places them.

The violin plot below shows the full standardized-return distribution for all 8
tickers side by side, so the departure from normal is visible everywhere, not only
at SPY.

```{python}
#| label: fig-violin-standardized
#| fig-cap: "Standardized daily log returns by ticker"

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.violinplot(
    data=returns_ridgeline, x="ticker", y="standardized_return", order=TICKERS,
    hue="ticker", palette=TICKER_COLORS, legend=False, inner="quartile", cut=0, ax=ax,
)
ax.set_xlabel(None)
ax.set_ylabel("Standardized daily log return")
add_title(ax, "Every Ticker Has Long, Thin Tails Reaching Past 5 Standard Deviations", "Standardized daily log returns by ticker")
fig.tight_layout()
```

Finally, the bar chart below distills each ticker's excess kurtosis, the single
number behind everything shown so far, into one ranked comparison. The result is not
the one a volatility-first intuition would predict.

```{python}
#| label: fig-kurtosis-ranking
#| fig-cap: "Excess kurtosis by ticker, sorted"

kurtosis_sorted = shape_table.sort_values("excess_kurtosis", ascending=False).reset_index(drop=True)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
bars = ax.bar(
    kurtosis_sorted["ticker"], kurtosis_sorted["excess_kurtosis"],
    color=[TICKER_COLORS[t] for t in kurtosis_sorted["ticker"]],
)
for bar, value in zip(bars, kurtosis_sorted["excess_kurtosis"]):
    ax.text(bar.get_x() + bar.get_width() / 2, bar.get_height() + 0.2, f"{value:.1f}", ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=10, color=COLOR_SECONDARY_INK)
ax.set_ylabel("Excess kurtosis")
add_title(ax, "SPY, Not TSLA, Has the Most Extreme Tail Risk", "Excess kurtosis by ticker: the index outranks every individual stock")
fig.tight_layout()
```

SPY has the highest excess kurtosis of all 8 tickers at 13.2, ahead of every
individual stock including TSLA, which has the lowest at 4.7. This runs against the
intuition that a single volatile stock should have the fattest tails; TSLA's high
day-to-day volatility (see the summary statistics table in Section 2) is spread more
evenly across many large moves, while SPY's crashes concentrate into a small number
of extraordinarily large single-day moves, like 2020-03-16, that a market-wide index
is more exposed to than any one company. High volatility and fat tails are related
but distinct properties, and this ranking is the clearest evidence in the report
that they do not always move together.

## Volatility Clustering

An iid-normal assumption implies constant volatility: today's variance is drawn from
the same distribution as tomorrow's, independent of what happened yesterday. This
section tests and visualizes whether that holds. Engle's ARCH-LM test [@engle1982]
formalizes the question directly, testing whether squared returns are
autocorrelated, which is exactly what "volatility depends on its own recent past"
means in statistical terms.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What is the ARCH-LM test?"}
ARCH-LM (Engle's Lagrange Multiplier test) checks for autocorrelation in a series'
squared values, which is what it means, statistically, for volatility to depend on
its own recent past. It works by fitting

$$
\varepsilon_t^2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \cdots + \alpha_p \varepsilon_{t-p}^2 + v_t
$$

on the return series' residuals $\varepsilon_t$ ($p = 10$ lags here) and testing
whether the $\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_p$ coefficients are jointly zero. A large test
statistic and small p-value reject that null, meaning past squared returns do help
predict today's squared return, the definition of an ARCH effect.
:::

```{python}
#| label: tbl-arch-lm
#| tbl-cap: "Engle's ARCH-LM test on SPY daily log returns (10 lags)"

spy_series = returns.loc[returns["ticker"] == "SPY"].sort_values("date").set_index("date")["log_return"]

lm_stat, lm_pvalue, f_stat, f_pvalue = het_arch(spy_series, nlags=10)
arch_lm_table = pd.DataFrame([{
    "lm_statistic": lm_stat, "lm_p_value": lm_pvalue,
    "f_statistic": f_stat, "f_p_value": f_pvalue,
}])

style_table(arch_lm_table, formats={
    "lm_statistic": "{:.1f}", "lm_p_value": "{:.2e}",
    "f_statistic": "{:.1f}", "f_p_value": "{:.2e}",
})
```

Both the LM and F versions of the test reject the null of no ARCH effects at any
conventional threshold (p far below 0.001). SPY's squared returns are
autocorrelated: large moves are statistically likely to be followed by more large
moves, regardless of direction. The chart below shows what that looks like as a
time series, SPY's 21-day rolling annualized volatility across the full window.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rolling-volatility
#| fig-cap: "SPY 21-day rolling annualized volatility"

spy_rolling_vol = spy_series.rolling(21).std() * np.sqrt(252)
peak_2020_date, peak_2020_val = spy_rolling_vol["2020"].idxmax(), spy_rolling_vol["2020"].max()
peak_2022_date, peak_2022_val = spy_rolling_vol["2022"].idxmax(), spy_rolling_vol["2022"].max()

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(spy_rolling_vol.index, spy_rolling_vol, color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], linewidth=1.2)
ax.axhline(spy_rolling_vol.median(), color=COLOR_MUTED, linestyle="--", linewidth=1, label="Full-window median (12.3%)")
ax.annotate(f"2020 COVID crash\n{peak_2020_val:.0%}", xy=(peak_2020_date, peak_2020_val), xytext=(12, 6), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9.5, color=COLOR_SECONDARY_INK)
ax.annotate(f"2022 rate hikes\n{peak_2022_val:.0%}", xy=(peak_2022_date, peak_2022_val), xytext=(12, 10), textcoords="offset points", fontsize=9.5, color=COLOR_SECONDARY_INK)
ax.set_ylim(0, spy_rolling_vol.max() * 1.2)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mticker.PercentFormatter(xmax=1))
ax.set_ylabel("21-day annualized volatility")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
add_title(ax, "SPY's Volatility Spiked to 94% in April 2020, 7.6x Its Typical Level", "21-day rolling annualized volatility of daily log returns")
fig.tight_layout()
```

The point of the ARCH-LM test is that this clustering is itself predictable from
recent history, not just visible in hindsight. A GARCH(1,1) model [@bollerslev1986],
fit here on SPY only as a single illustrative example rather than a full model
comparison, lets volatility depend on yesterday's shock and yesterday's variance.
The chart below overlays its conditional volatility against the realized rolling
volatility from
above.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What is a GARCH(1,1) model?"}
GARCH(1,1) (Generalized AutoRegressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity) models
today's variance as a weighted combination of three things: a long-run baseline
level, yesterday's squared shock, and yesterday's variance itself:

$$
\sigma_t^2 = \omega + \alpha\, \varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + \beta\, \sigma_{t-1}^2
$$

$\omega$ is the baseline variance level, $\alpha$ is how much yesterday's surprise
$\varepsilon_{t-1}^2$ moves today's variance, and $\beta$ is how much volatility
persists on its own from $\sigma_{t-1}^2$. The sum $\alpha + \beta$ measures
persistence: the closer it is to 1, the more slowly a volatility shock decays. In
the SPY fit used here, $\alpha \approx 0.17$ and $\beta \approx 0.79$, so
$\alpha + \beta \approx 0.96$, which is why a single day of memory in each direction
reproduces most of the clustering pattern visible in the realized volatility chart
above.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-garch-overlay
#| fig-cap: "SPY realized rolling volatility vs. GARCH(1,1) conditional volatility"

garch_model = arch_model(spy_series * 100, vol="Garch", p=1, q=1, dist="normal")
garch_result = garch_model.fit(disp="off")
garch_cond_vol = garch_result.conditional_volatility / 100 * np.sqrt(252)

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(spy_rolling_vol.index, spy_rolling_vol, color=COLOR_MUTED, linewidth=1.1, label="Realized (21-day rolling)")
ax.plot(garch_cond_vol.index, garch_cond_vol, color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], linewidth=1.1, label="GARCH(1,1) conditional")
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mticker.PercentFormatter(xmax=1))
ax.set_ylabel("Annualized volatility")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
add_title(ax, "A One-Day-Memory Model Tracks SPY's Volatility Swings Closely", "GARCH(1,1) conditional volatility needs only yesterday's shock and variance")
fig.tight_layout()
```

The fitted model's persistence parameters, $\alpha \approx 0.17$ and
$\beta \approx 0.79$, sum to $\alpha + \beta \approx 0.96$: today's variance is a
weighted blend of yesterday's shock and yesterday's variance, and that blend barely
decays, which is why the conditional volatility line
tracks the realized line's spikes and calm periods so closely without ever seeing
tomorrow's return. This is the concrete mechanism behind "volatility clustering":
a model using only one lag of memory reproduces most of the pattern an iid-normal
assumption says should not exist at all.

Is this an SPY-specific pattern, or does every ticker's volatility cluster the same
way? The chart below overlays 21-day rolling annualized volatility for all 8
tickers on one axis.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rolling-volatility-all
#| fig-cap: "21-day rolling annualized volatility, all 8 tickers"

rolling_vol_all = (
    returns.set_index("date").groupby("ticker")["log_return"]
    .rolling(21).std().mul(np.sqrt(252)).reset_index()
)
rolling_vol_wide = rolling_vol_all.pivot(index="date", columns="ticker", values="log_return")

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for ticker in TICKERS:
    ax.plot(rolling_vol_wide.index, rolling_vol_wide[ticker], color=TICKER_COLORS[ticker], linewidth=1, alpha=0.85, label=ticker)
ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(mticker.PercentFormatter(xmax=1))
ax.set_ylabel("21-day annualized volatility")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", ncol=4)
add_title(ax, "TSLA's Typical Volatility Is 4x SPY's, Every Single Year", "21-day rolling annualized volatility, all 8 tickers")
fig.tight_layout()
```

Every ticker's volatility rises and falls together around 2020 and 2022, confirming
the clustering shown for SPY is a market-wide pattern, not an index-specific one.
TSLA sits visibly above the other 7 tickers almost everywhere on this chart; its
median rolling volatility across the full window is 49.2%, almost exactly 4 times
SPY's median of 12.3%.

The heatmap below makes the ticker-by-ticker, year-by-year pattern explicit:
annualized volatility for all 8 tickers, one row per ticker, one column per
calendar year.

```{python}
#| label: fig-volatility-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Annualized volatility by ticker and year"

returns_with_year = returns.copy()
returns_with_year["year"] = returns_with_year["date"].dt.year
vol_by_year = (
    returns_with_year.groupby(["ticker", "year"])["log_return"]
    .std().mul(np.sqrt(252)).unstack("year").reindex(TICKERS)
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(13, 5.5))
sns.heatmap(
    vol_by_year, annot=True, fmt=".0%", cmap=sns.light_palette(SEQUENTIAL_RAMP[3], as_cmap=True),
    linewidths=1, linecolor=COLOR_SURFACE, cbar_kws={"label": "Annualized volatility"}, ax=ax,
)
ax.set_xlabel(None)
ax.set_ylabel(None)
add_title(ax, "TSLA Runs Hot Every Year; the Rest Only Spike in Crisis Years", "Annualized volatility by ticker and calendar year")
fig.tight_layout()
```

TSLA's row is the warmest almost everywhere on the map, ranging from 39% to 67%
across every single year in the window, including calm years for every other
ticker. The other 7 tickers tell a different story: mostly muted, with 2020 and
2022 standing out as visibly hotter columns across nearly every row at once, more
than doubling the pre-2020 baseline on average (48% average across all 8 tickers in
2020 against a 24% baseline in the other years). That is the same distinction
Section 4 raised in kurtosis terms: TSLA's risk is spread evenly across time, so its
excess kurtosis is the lowest of the 8, while the other tickers are normally calm
but occasionally shocked hard enough, in the same years, to produce the fattest
tails in the set.

## Autocorrelation of Returns

An iid assumption implies no autocorrelation at any lag, for the raw returns or for
their magnitude: today's return should carry no statistical information about
tomorrow's. This section tests both directly. The Ljung-Box test [@ljungbox1978]
checks a series for autocorrelation jointly across a block of lags rather than one
lag at a time.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What is the Ljung-Box test?"}
The Ljung-Box test checks whether a series has any autocorrelation across a block of
lags at once, rather than testing each lag separately, which avoids inflating the
false-positive rate that would come from running many single-lag tests side by side.
The statistic is

$$
Q = n(n+2) \sum_{k=1}^{h} \frac{\hat{\rho}_k^2}{n-k}
$$

where $n$ is the sample size, $h$ is the number of lags tested (10 in this report),
and $\hat{\rho}_k$ is the sample autocorrelation at lag $k$. $Q$ is compared against
a chi-square distribution with $h$ degrees of freedom; a large $Q$ and small p-value
reject the null that all $h$ autocorrelations are jointly zero.
:::

```{python}
#| label: tbl-ljung-box
#| tbl-cap: "Ljung-Box test (10 lags) on raw and squared daily log returns"

ljung_box_results = []
for ticker in TICKERS:
    series = returns.loc[returns["ticker"] == ticker, "log_return"]
    lb_raw = acorr_ljungbox(series, lags=[10], return_df=True)
    lb_squared = acorr_ljungbox(series**2, lags=[10], return_df=True)
    ljung_box_results.append({
        "ticker": ticker,
        "raw_statistic": lb_raw["lb_stat"].iloc[0],
        "raw_p": lb_raw["lb_pvalue"].iloc[0],
        "squared_statistic": lb_squared["lb_stat"].iloc[0],
        "squared_p": lb_squared["lb_pvalue"].iloc[0],
    })

ljung_box_table = pd.DataFrame(ljung_box_results)

style_table(ljung_box_table, formats={
    "raw_statistic": "{:.1f}", "raw_p": "{:.4f}",
    "squared_statistic": "{:,.1f}", "squared_p": "{:.4f}",
})
```

Testing 8 tickers against 2 series (raw and squared returns) is 16 tests at once,
so the same multiplicity discipline from Section 4 applies: judged against a
Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.05 divided by 16, or 0.003125, every squared-
return result still rejects independence by many orders of magnitude. The raw-return
results are more mixed: 6 of 8 tickers clear even the strict threshold, XOM's raw
p-value of 0.0007 clears 0.003125 as well, and TSLA is the one exception, with a raw
p-value of 0.7968 that does not reject independence at any threshold. Even where raw
returns are significant, the test statistics are dramatically smaller than their
squared-return counterparts, SPY's 164.6 against 3,916.4, for example, showing that
whatever autocorrelation exists in the raw returns is a much weaker effect than the
volatility clustering in their magnitude.

The chart below shows why SPY's raw-return test rejects independence: the ACF and
PACF plots of SPY's raw daily log returns, both against the approximate 95%
confidence band a white-noise series would fall inside.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="How to read an ACF/PACF plot"}
Both plots show correlation on the y-axis against lag (in trading days) on the
x-axis. The ACF (autocorrelation function) shows the raw correlation between a
series and its own value $k$ days earlier, for each lag $k$. The PACF (partial
autocorrelation function) shows the same relationship after removing the part
already explained by shorter lags, isolating what each additional lag adds on its
own. The shaded band marks the approximate 95% confidence interval under the null
of no autocorrelation, roughly $\pm 1.96/\sqrt{n}$; a bar extending outside the band
is a lag with statistically significant autocorrelation.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-acf-pacf-raw
#| fig-cap: "ACF and PACF of SPY daily log returns"

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))
plot_acf(spy_series, lags=15, ax=axes[0], title=None, color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], vlines_kwargs={"colors": TICKER_COLORS["SPY"]})
plot_pacf(spy_series, lags=15, ax=axes[1], title=None, color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], vlines_kwargs={"colors": TICKER_COLORS["SPY"]}, method="ywm")
for ax, label in zip(axes, ["ACF", "PACF"]):
    for coll in ax.collections:
        if "Poly" in type(coll).__name__:
            coll.set_facecolor(COLOR_GRID)
    ax.set_title(label, loc="left", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=COLOR_SECONDARY_INK, pad=6)
    ax.set_xlabel("Lag (trading days)")
    ax.set_ylim(-0.15, 0.15)

fig.suptitle("A Small but Real Negative Autocorrelation Shows Up at Lag 1", x=0.01, y=0.99, ha="left", va="top", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=COLOR_PRIMARY_INK)
fig.text(0.01, 0.90, "SPY daily log returns, 15 lags (lag 0 cut off at 1.0), shaded band is the 95% white-noise confidence interval", fontsize=10.5, color=COLOR_SECONDARY_INK)
fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.82])
```

Lag 1 carries a -0.105 autocorrelation, well outside the confidence band and the
largest single value in either plot, consistent with short-term mean reversion or
microstructure effects like bid-ask bounce. A handful of later lags (2, 6, 7, 8, and
9) poke outside the band too, but none as large as lag 1, and several lags inside
the first 15 stay within it entirely. This is a real but modest effect, nowhere near
the pattern the next chart shows for squared returns.

```{python}
#| label: fig-acf-squared
#| fig-cap: "ACF of SPY squared daily log returns"

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
plot_acf(spy_series**2, lags=15, ax=ax, title=None, color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], vlines_kwargs={"colors": TICKER_COLORS["SPY"]})
for coll in ax.collections:
    if "Poly" in type(coll).__name__:
        coll.set_facecolor(COLOR_GRID)
ax.set_xlabel("Lag (trading days)")
ax.set_ylabel("Autocorrelation")
add_title(ax, "Squared Returns Stay Autocorrelated Past 15 Trading Days", "ACF of SPY squared daily log returns")
fig.tight_layout()
```

Every one of the first 15 lags sits outside the confidence band, starting at 0.41
at lag 1 and still at 0.15 by lag 15, decaying far more slowly than anything in the
raw-return ACF. This is the same volatility clustering from Section 5 expressed as
an autocorrelation statistic instead of a rolling-window chart: large moves predict
more large moves, in either direction, for well over two trading weeks.

The scatter plots below make the ACF's lag-1 story concrete: SPY's return against
the prior day's return, and the same comparison using absolute values.

```{python}
#| label: fig-lag-scatter
#| fig-cap: "SPY: return_t vs. return_t-1 (left) and |return_t| vs. |return_t-1| (right)"

spy_lagged = pd.DataFrame({"return_t": spy_series, "return_t_minus_1": spy_series.shift(1)}).dropna()

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5.5))
axes[0].scatter(spy_lagged["return_t_minus_1"], spy_lagged["return_t"], s=8, color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], alpha=0.3)
axes[0].set_xlabel(r"return$_{t-1}$")
axes[0].set_ylabel(r"return$_t$")
axes[0].set_title("Raw returns", loc="left", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=COLOR_SECONDARY_INK, pad=6)

axes[1].scatter(spy_lagged["return_t_minus_1"].abs(), spy_lagged["return_t"].abs(), s=8, color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], alpha=0.3)
axes[1].set_xlabel(r"|return$_{t-1}$|")
axes[1].set_ylabel(r"|return$_t$|")
axes[1].set_title("Absolute returns", loc="left", fontsize=11, fontweight="bold", color=COLOR_SECONDARY_INK, pad=6)

fig.suptitle("No Visible Pattern in Direction, a Clear One in Magnitude", x=0.01, ha="left", fontsize=14, fontweight="bold", color=COLOR_PRIMARY_INK)
fig.text(0.01, 0.93, "SPY daily log returns, one trading day apart", fontsize=10.5, color=COLOR_SECONDARY_INK)
fig.tight_layout(rect=[0, 0, 1, 0.88])
```

The left panel is close to a shapeless cloud, consistent with a weak, easy-to-miss
lag-1 effect rather than an obvious visual pattern. The right panel is visibly
cone-shaped: points cluster tightly near the origin regardless of the prior day's
size, but the spread of possible same-day moves widens noticeably as the prior
day's move grows, exactly what a positive autocorrelation in magnitude, and
nothing equivalent in direction, looks like on a scatter plot.

Finally, the heatmap below summarizes the full Ljung-Box results table as a single
image, all 8 tickers against both series.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ljung-box-heatmap
#| fig-cap: "Ljung-Box p-values, all 8 tickers, raw vs. squared returns"

ljung_box_pvalues = ljung_box_table.set_index("ticker")[["raw_p", "squared_p"]].reindex(TICKERS)
ljung_box_pvalues.columns = ["Raw returns", "Squared returns"]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 6))
sns.heatmap(
    ljung_box_pvalues, annot=True, fmt=".4f", cmap=sns.light_palette(SEQUENTIAL_RAMP[3], as_cmap=True),
    vmin=0, vmax=1, linewidths=1, linecolor=COLOR_SURFACE, cbar_kws={"label": "p-value"}, ax=ax,
)
ax.set_xlabel(None)
ax.set_ylabel(None)
add_title(ax, "TSLA Is the Only Ticker Whose Raw Returns Aren't Autocorrelated", "Ljung-Box p-values (10 lags), all 8 tickers")
fig.tight_layout()
```

TSLA's raw-return cell is the one visibly light square on the map, a p-value of
0.797 against a column of values under 0.001 everywhere else. Its squared-return
cell tells the opposite story: p effectively 0, same as every other ticker. TSLA is
the ticker whose day-to-day direction is closest to genuinely unpredictable from its
own past, and it is simultaneously as volatility-clustered as anything else in the
set, a reminder that "returns are unpredictable" and "volatility is unpredictable"
are different claims, and only the second one holds without exception here.

## What This Means for Value-at-Risk

Every section so far has shown a way daily returns depart from an iid-normal
assumption: fat tails, volatility that clusters instead of staying constant, and
autocorrelation in return magnitude. This section quantifies what that costs a risk
model built on the normal assumption, using Value-at-Risk, one of the most common
risk measures in finance.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What is Value-at-Risk (VaR)?"}
VaR answers one question: how much could a position lose over a given period, with a
given confidence level. A 1-day 99% VaR of $20,000 on a $1M position means the model
expects a loss larger than $20,000 on no more than 1% of trading days, 1-in-100 days.
It says nothing about how large the loss could be on that worst 1%, only where the
threshold sits. This report computes VaR two ways: a normal VaR, which assumes
returns are normally distributed with the recent sample mean and standard deviation,
and a historical (empirical) VaR, which uses the recent sample's actual worst
returns directly, with no distributional assumption at all.
:::

To avoid a subtle problem, testing a VaR method against the exact same data used to
calibrate it, both VaR methods here are computed on a rolling basis: each day's
threshold uses only the trailing 252 trading days (about one calendar year) ending
the day before, so every breach check is a genuine out-of-sample test, never a
threshold looking at its own future.

```{python}
#| label: var-functions
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show VaR and backtest functions"

def rolling_var_thresholds(series, alpha, window=252):
    mu = series.rolling(window).mean().shift(1)
    sigma = series.rolling(window).std().shift(1)
    z = stats.norm.ppf(alpha)
    normal_threshold = mu + z * sigma
    historical_threshold = series.rolling(window).quantile(alpha).shift(1)
    return normal_threshold, historical_threshold


def kupiec_pof_test(n, x, p):
    if x == 0:
        lr = -2 * n * np.log(1 - p)
    else:
        phat = x / n
        lr = -2 * (x * np.log(p) + (n - x) * np.log(1 - p) - x * np.log(phat) - (n - x) * np.log(1 - phat))
    return lr, 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(lr, df=1)


def christoffersen_independence_test(breach_series):
    b = breach_series.astype(int).to_numpy()
    n00 = n01 = n10 = n11 = 0
    for i in range(1, len(b)):
        prev, cur = b[i - 1], b[i]
        if prev == 0 and cur == 0:
            n00 += 1
        elif prev == 0 and cur == 1:
            n01 += 1
        elif prev == 1 and cur == 0:
            n10 += 1
        else:
            n11 += 1
    pi01 = n01 / (n00 + n01) if (n00 + n01) > 0 else 0
    pi11 = n11 / (n10 + n11) if (n10 + n11) > 0 else 0
    pi = (n01 + n11) / (n00 + n01 + n10 + n11)

    def safe_log(x):
        return np.log(x) if x > 0 else 0

    ll_restricted = (n01 + n11) * safe_log(pi) + (n00 + n10) * safe_log(1 - pi)
    ll_unrestricted = n00 * safe_log(1 - pi01) + n01 * safe_log(pi01) + n10 * safe_log(1 - pi11) + n11 * safe_log(pi11)
    lr = -2 * (ll_restricted - ll_unrestricted)
    return lr, 1 - stats.chi2.cdf(lr, df=1)
```

The table below runs both VaR methods at both the 95% and 99% confidence levels for
SPY, backtests each against SPY's actual realized returns, and reports the observed
breach rate against the nominal rate, alongside Kupiec's Proportion-of-Failures test
[@kupiec1995] and Christoffersen's independence test [@christoffersen1998].

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="What do Kupiec's and Christoffersen's tests check?"}
Both tests examine the sequence of breaches (days where the actual loss exceeded the
VaR threshold) but check different things. Kupiec's Proportion-of-Failures test asks
whether the *overall rate* of breaches matches the nominal rate the VaR level
promises:

$$
LR_{POF} = -2 \ln \left( \frac{p^{x} (1-p)^{n-x}}{\hat{p}^{x} (1-\hat{p})^{n-x}} \right)
$$

where $n$ is the number of observations, $x$ is the number of breaches, $p$ is the
nominal breach rate (0.01 for 99% VaR), and $\hat{p} = x/n$ is the observed rate.
$LR_{POF}$ follows a chi-square distribution with 1 degree of freedom; a large value
means the observed breach rate is significantly different from what the model
promised. Christoffersen's independence test instead asks whether breaches are
*independent over time* rather than clustering together, using the transition
counts $n_{ij}$ between consecutive days' breach/no-breach states:

$$
LR_{ind} = -2 \ln \left( \frac{(1-\pi)^{n_{00}+n_{10}} \pi^{n_{01}+n_{11}}}{(1-\pi_{01})^{n_{00}} \pi_{01}^{n_{01}} (1-\pi_{11})^{n_{10}} \pi_{11}^{n_{11}}} \right)
$$

where $\pi_{01}$ and $\pi_{11}$ are the probabilities of a breach today given no
breach or a breach yesterday, and $\pi$ is the overall breach rate. A model can pass
Kupiec (the right average rate) while failing Christoffersen (breaches still arrive
in clusters), which is exactly the pattern volatility clustering would predict.
:::

```{python}
#| label: tbl-var-backtest
#| tbl-cap: "SPY VaR backtest: 95% and 99%, normal vs. historical, rolling 252-day window"

var_backtest_results = []
for level, alpha in [("95%", 0.05), ("99%", 0.01)]:
    normal_thr, hist_thr = rolling_var_thresholds(spy_series, alpha)
    valid = normal_thr.notna()
    actual, normal_thr, hist_thr = spy_series[valid], normal_thr[valid], hist_thr[valid]
    n = len(actual)
    for method, threshold in [("Normal", normal_thr), ("Historical", hist_thr)]:
        breach = actual < threshold
        x = int(breach.sum())
        lr_pof, p_pof = kupiec_pof_test(n, x, alpha)
        lr_ind, p_ind = christoffersen_independence_test(breach)
        var_backtest_results.append({
            "level": level, "method": method, "n": n, "breaches": x,
            "breach_rate": x / n, "nominal_rate": alpha,
            "kupiec_lr": lr_pof, "kupiec_p": p_pof,
            "christoffersen_lr": lr_ind, "christoffersen_p": p_ind,
        })

var_backtest_table = pd.DataFrame(var_backtest_results)

style_table(var_backtest_table, formats={
    "n": "{:,.0f}", "breaches": "{:.0f}",
    "breach_rate": "{:.2%}", "nominal_rate": "{:.0%}",
    "kupiec_lr": "{:.2f}", "kupiec_p": "{:.4f}",
    "christoffersen_lr": "{:.2f}", "christoffersen_p": "{:.4f}",
})
```

At 95%, both methods land close to their 5% nominal rate (normal 5.27%, historical
4.92%) and Kupiec does not reject either. At 99%, the picture changes sharply:
normal VaR breaches 2.57% of the time against a 1% promise, and Kupiec rejects that
gap overwhelmingly (p effectively 0, unaffected by any correction); historical VaR
breaches 1.46% of the time, still above nominal but a much smaller miss, and Kupiec
rejects more narrowly, at p = 0.0085. This table runs 8 test statistics total (2
methods x 2 levels x {Kupiec, Christoffersen}), and that one result is the single
borderline case: judged against a Bonferroni-adjusted threshold of 0.05 divided by
8 (0.00625), historical VaR's 99% Kupiec rejection does not survive. Every other
result in the table is either already non-significant (both 95% Kupiec tests) or
significant by many orders of magnitude (everything else), so this correction
narrows one specific claim, historical VaR's 99% calibration is a real but fragile
miss, rather than changing the report's central findings, which rest on the
normal-VaR failure and the universal Christoffersen rejections, neither of which is
close to the corrected threshold. Christoffersen rejects independence for every
method at every level, including the two cases that passed Kupiec: even when the
average breach rate looks correct, breaches still cluster in time rather than
landing independently, the same volatility-clustering signature from Sections 5 and
6 showing up again, this time inside a risk model's own failures.

The chart below shows the 99% story directly: SPY's daily returns against both
rolling VaR thresholds, with each method's breaches marked.

```{python}
#| label: fig-var-threshold-overlay
#| fig-cap: "SPY daily returns vs. rolling 99% VaR thresholds, normal and historical"

normal_thr_99, hist_thr_99 = rolling_var_thresholds(spy_series, 0.01)
valid_99 = normal_thr_99.notna()
actual_99, normal_thr_99, hist_thr_99 = spy_series[valid_99], normal_thr_99[valid_99], hist_thr_99[valid_99]
normal_breach_99 = actual_99 < normal_thr_99
hist_breach_99 = actual_99 < hist_thr_99

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(actual_99.index, actual_99, color=COLOR_GRID, linewidth=0.7, zorder=1)
ax.plot(normal_thr_99.index, normal_thr_99, color=COLOR_MUTED, linewidth=1.3, linestyle="--", label="Normal 99% VaR threshold", zorder=2)
ax.plot(hist_thr_99.index, hist_thr_99, color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], linewidth=1.3, label="Historical 99% VaR threshold", zorder=2)
ax.scatter(actual_99.index[normal_breach_99], actual_99[normal_breach_99], facecolor="none", edgecolor="#d03b3b", linewidth=1.1, s=32, zorder=3, label="Normal VaR breach")
ax.scatter(actual_99.index[hist_breach_99], actual_99[hist_breach_99], color="#d03b3b", s=22, marker="x", linewidth=1.4, zorder=3, label="Historical VaR breach")
ax.set_ylabel("Daily log return")
ax.legend(loc="lower left", ncol=2, fontsize=9)
add_title(ax, "At the 99% Level, Normal VaR Breaches 2.6x Too Often", "Rolling 252-day 99% VaR thresholds vs. actual SPY daily returns")
fig.tight_layout()
```

Both threshold lines drift wider during 2020 and 2022 as the trailing 252-day window
picks up the higher realized volatility from Section 5, but they only adapt after
the fact: the sharpest breaches (the light gray dots furthest below the dashed line)
cluster right at the start of the 2020 crash, exactly when a slow-to-adapt threshold
is most exposed. The chart below turns the same breach data into a running count.

```{python}
#| label: fig-var-cumulative-breaches
#| fig-cap: "Cumulative 99% VaR breaches over time, normal vs. historical"

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(actual_99.index, normal_breach_99.cumsum(), color=COLOR_MUTED, linewidth=1.6, label="Normal VaR")
ax.plot(actual_99.index, hist_breach_99.cumsum(), color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], linewidth=1.6, label="Historical VaR")
ax.set_ylabel("Cumulative breach count")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
add_title(ax, "Normal VaR's Shortfall Builds for a Decade, Then Stalls", "Cumulative 99% VaR breaches over time")
fig.tight_layout()
```

The gap between the two lines opens gradually rather than in one crisis jump: 8
breaches by the end of 2014, 23 by 2018, 41 by the end of 2022, widening in nearly
every multi-year stretch along the way rather than sitting flat until a single
shock. From 2022 onward, though, the gap holds exactly at 41: both methods add 12
more breaches apiece through the end of the window, tracking each other closely.
Normal VaR's shortfall against historical VaR here is a legacy of the 2011-2022
period specifically, not an ongoing trend, at least not yet.

Is SPY's 99% normal-VaR overshoot a fluke of one ticker, or does the same failure
show up everywhere in the set? The chart below runs the identical rolling backtest
on all 8 tickers and plots each method's actual breach rate as a multiple of the 1%
nominal rate.

```{python}
#| label: fig-var-cross-ticker
#| fig-cap: "99% VaR breach rate as a multiple of the 1% nominal rate, all 8 tickers"

cross_ticker_var = []
for ticker in TICKERS:
    series = returns.loc[returns["ticker"] == ticker].sort_values("date").set_index("date")["log_return"]
    normal_thr, hist_thr = rolling_var_thresholds(series, 0.01)
    valid = normal_thr.notna()
    actual, normal_thr, hist_thr = series[valid], normal_thr[valid], hist_thr[valid]
    cross_ticker_var.append({
        "ticker": ticker,
        "normal_ratio": (actual < normal_thr).mean() / 0.01,
        "historical_ratio": (actual < hist_thr).mean() / 0.01,
    })
cross_ticker_var = pd.DataFrame(cross_ticker_var)

x_pos = np.arange(len(TICKERS))
width = 0.38

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.bar(x_pos - width / 2, cross_ticker_var["normal_ratio"], width, color=COLOR_MUTED, label="Normal VaR")
ax.bar(x_pos + width / 2, cross_ticker_var["historical_ratio"], width, color=TICKER_COLORS["SPY"], label="Historical VaR")
ax.axhline(1.0, color=COLOR_PRIMARY_INK, linewidth=1, linestyle=":", label="Perfectly calibrated")
ax.set_xticks(x_pos)
ax.set_xticklabels(TICKERS)
ax.set_ylabel("Actual breach rate / 1% nominal rate")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
add_title(ax, "Normal VaR Overshoots Its Own 1% Target on Every Single Ticker", "99% VaR breach rate as a multiple of the nominal rate, all 8 tickers")
fig.tight_layout()
```

Every normal-VaR bar sits above every historical-VaR bar, and every bar of either
color sits above the dotted 1.0 line: no ticker's 99% VaR is well calibrated by
either method, though historical VaR is consistently closer. TSLA has the smallest
overshoot on both methods (1.78x and 1.24x), consistent with it also having this
report's lowest excess kurtosis in Section 4.

Averaged across the rolling backtest window, SPY's normal 99% VaR threshold implies
a 1-day loss of $22,921 on a $1M position; the historical 99% VaR threshold implies
$28,673, a $5,752 gap, 25% larger than what the normal model reports. A risk desk
sizing capital or margin off the normal number alone would be short by roughly a
quarter of the loss the data itself says to expect at that confidence level, before
even accounting for the breach-clustering problem Christoffersen's test surfaced
above, which affects both methods and means the shortfall is not spread evenly
across time but concentrated in exactly the crisis windows, 2020 and 2022, when
capital is most needed.
